identification.title: I Surrender All
identification.artist: Judson W. Van DeVenter and Winfield S. Weeden
identification.notes: Words by Judson W. Van DeVenter (1855-1939), music by Winfield S. Weeden (1847-1908); first published in 1896 in Gospel Songs of Grace and Glory (Sebring Publishing, New York). Van DeVenter wrote it at George Sebring's home in East Palestine, Ohio, to mark his own decision to give his life to full-time ministry, after about five years of hesitation. Public domain. The list's guess of the hymn is right. It is widely recorded and was made familiar by Billy Graham's crusades, who studied under Van DeVenter; a fifth stanza is often omitted. Reviewed as the hymn as congregations sing it, not as any one recording.

claims.structuralNotes: Five stanzas, each followed by the same refrain of full surrender. Stanza 1 gives all to Jesus in love and trust. Stanza 2 bows humbly, forsakes worldly pleasure and asks Jesus to take the singer now. Stanza 3 asks to be made wholly his, to feel the Holy Spirit and to know that he belongs to Christ. Stanza 4 gives the self and asks to be filled with God's love and power and blessing. Stanza 5 reports a felt flame, the joy of full salvation and glory to his name. The voice is first person singular throughout and the subject is the singer's own consecration and experience. Christ and the Spirit are named; the cross and resurrection are never narrated, so the gospel is the unspoken ground.

claims.claim: The singer gives everything to Jesus freely and resolves to love and trust him and live in his presence daily.
claims.subject: Consecration

claims.claim: The singer bows humbly, forsakes worldly pleasure and asks Jesus to take him now.
claims.subject: Devotion to Christ

claims.claim: The singer asks to be made wholly Christ's, to feel the Holy Spirit and to know that he belongs to Christ.
claims.subject: The Spirit and assurance

claims.claim: The singer gives himself and asks to be filled with God's love and power and to receive his blessing.
claims.subject: Dedication and filling

claims.claim: The singer reports a felt fire, the joy of full salvation, and gives glory to Christ's name.
claims.subject: Joy in salvation

claims.claim: Each stanza ends by repeating total surrender to the Savior.
claims.subject: Total surrender

strengths.title: Surrender as the Christian's whole posture
strengths.explanation: The hymn puts the call of total allegiance to Christ in a congregation's mouth: nothing held back, Christ first. It is the standing response of the redeemed rather than a means of earning anything.
strengths.scriptureRationale: Presenting the whole self as a living sacrifice in response to God's mercies - the consecration the refrain repeats.

strengths.title: Dependence on God for the surrendered life
strengths.explanation: The singer asks to know the Holy Spirit's presence and to be filled with God's love and power, so surrender is not left to resolve alone. That qualifies the song's own centre of gravity.
strengths.scriptureRationale: Walking by the Spirit rather than the flesh - the dependence the stanzas voice.

strengths.title: Joy in being saved
strengths.explanation: The closing stanza ends in joy and glory given to Christ's name, which turns the surrender toward praise rather than strain.
strengths.scriptureRationale: Joy of salvation restored - the gladness the last stanza voices.

doctrinesAffirmed: Lordship of Christ over the whole life
theological.assessment: No false statement. The hymn is a testimonial prayer of consecration. It names no act of God, so the reason for surrender (the cross) is assumed, and the singer's resolve and felt experience are its subject. The words 'full salvation' and feeling a flame come from the holiness tradition; read plainly they voice joy in Christ, so they are noted here, not counted as error. Sung beside a song of the cross it is sound.

strengths.title: A response song with a long church life
strengths.explanation: Churches have used it as an invitation and a song of dedication for over a century, and its refrain is simple enough for a room to hold from memory.

strengths.title: A short, memorable refrain
strengths.explanation: The refrain is easy to learn, so a congregation can join on first hearing.

communal.vocalRangeNote: Commonly printed in the flat keys; a mid-range gospel melody that most mixed congregations manage. Check against the leader's key and the arrangement used.

range.key: Varies by hymnal; no key verified
range.note: No chart was read for this review, so the pitches are not stated.

communal.repetitionAssessment: A fixed refrain returns after each stanza and gathers the stanza's particular surrender into one confession.
communal.assessment: Strophic, congregational and easy to sing. The singular voice fits a prayer of commitment, but each singer confesses his own resolve and feeling, so the room speaks personal testimony, not a shared creed. It suits a response moment after the gospel has been preached or sung.

strengths.title: A single clear idea
strengths.explanation: The song says one thing and says it plainly, so there is little to misread.

clarity.assessment: Clear in what it asks. It does not say why Christ is worthy of surrender or what he did; a hearer unfamiliar with the gospel would not learn it here. The felt-flame language is the one place a newcomer may be unsure what is meant.

synthesis.summary: A 1896 gospel hymn of personal consecration over five stanzas: the singer yields all to Jesus, forsakes the world, asks to know the Spirit and be filled with love and power, and ends in the joy of full salvation. The voice is the singer's own resolve and experience, not a credal confession. No false statement was found. It names no act of God, so the cross is assumed, not sung.

scriptureReferences.relevance: Presenting oneself wholly to God in view of his mercies - the hymn's central act.
Denying oneself and following Christ daily - the call of full allegiance.
Walking by the Spirit - the dependence the Spirit stanza voices.
